title: 12 Cursor rules that stop AI assistants writing outdated FastAPI code
author: RDJ
summary: AI coding assistants still reach for FastAPI patterns from a few years ago: .dict() , orm_mode , session.query() , HTTPException raised deep inside service code, SQLite in tests. The code runs, but it isn't the code you'd write today. Cursor's project rules fix most of this. A rule is a small .mdc file in .cursor/rules/ with a glob, so it loads only when you edit matching files: --- description : " FastAPI routers, dependencies and Pydantic v2 schemas" globs : src/app/**/router.py,src/app/**/schemas.py,src/app/**/deps.py alwaysApply : false --- - One APIRouter(prefix="/<plural-resource>") per feature ... These are the 12 conventions that made the biggest difference for me. Routers and schemas Pydantic v2 APIs only. model_validate , model_dump , ConfigDict , field_validator . Never .dict() , parse_obj , orm_mode , class Config or the v1 validator decorator. Routers are thin and async. Parse, call a service, return a schema. No SQL or business rules in routers. Always declare response_model (or a return annotation) and an explicit status_code : 201 for create, 204 for delete. Schemas are named XCreate / XUpdate / XRead . Input models use ConfigDict(extra="forbid") so a sneaky "is_admin": true is rejected. Apply updates with model_dump(exclude_unset=True) . Database SQLAlchemy 2.0 style only. Mapped[...] , mapped_column() , select() . Never session.query() or declarative_base() . Services own the transaction with async with session.begin(): . Repositories never commit. Use async_sessionmaker(expire_on_commit=False) . Relationships default to lazy="raise" . Load explicitly with selectinload() or joinedload() , so there's no hidden IO in async code. Set MetaData(naming_convention=...) on your Base so Alembic constraint names are deterministic. Never edit a migration that's already applied. Errors, config and safety Services raise your own AppError subclasses, never HTTPException . One exception handler maps them to {"error": {"code": ..., "message": ...}} . Settings only through a cached get_settings() built on pydantic-settings. Never read os.environ elsewhere, and keep secrets as SecretStr . Never build SQL with f-strings. Use bound parameters or text(...).bindparams() . Tests pytest + pytest-asyncio + httpx.AsyncClient(transport=ASGITransport(app=app)) , against a real Postgres with a rollback per test. Clear app.dependency_overrides after each test. No SQLite stand-in. Using them Drop rules like these into .cursor/rules/ , one file per area, with globs that match your layout. For Claude Code, the same conventions work as a short CLAUDE.md at the repo root. Disclosure: I made a FastAPI rules pack with these conventions written out as 7 scoped .mdc files plus a CLAUDE.md , and I sell it for $12 at codebaserules.com . Two of the files are a free download , no email needed. Everything above works without buying anything. I'd like to hear which of these you'd change.

title: An approval was corrected to Declined: how to test permission revocation
author: murray wang
summary: Your fixture session received Approved and granted a local permission. A later event says Declined. You need to decide whether that event revokes access, and how to tell a real correction from a replayed or stale callback. This article tests that decision in the synthetic fixture and separates what the fixture does from what your application must design. The problem: an approval that no longer holds A seller passed verification, your handler recorded Approved, and the explicit policy allowed a local permission. Later a new Declined event arrives for the same session. If your code treats every terminal status as final, it ignores the correction and access stays open. If it treats every incoming event as fresh, a replayed callback can flip state back and forth. The goal is narrow. A new Declined correction after Approved must set permission_granted from true to false. grant_count must stay at 1, because the history of the grant does not disappear. Duplicate and stale events must change nothing. Whether a real provider ever sends such corrections, and what they mean, depends on that provider's actual contract. The fixture only lets you rehearse the shape. What the fixture actually implements The downloadable identity example stores sessions and processed event IDs in SQLite. Its event method accepts only mode synthetic_fixture and source fixture_callback, and only event IDs that start with fixture-. It has no production signature verifier. It checks tenant and subject binding first, then deduplicates on the session and event ID pair. One rule handles corrections. If the stored status is approved and the incoming status is Declined, the fixture records the event and sets status to declined and granted to 0. It leaves the grants counter untouched. Any other event against an approved, declined or expired session returns the current state unchanged. That event is not recorded either. This correction check runs before the deadline check, so a Declined correction after Approved is applied even when it arrives after the deadline. live_permission_changed is always false. No real permission exists. Hypothetical scenario and expected outputs This is a hypothetical walkthrough on fixture-session, bound to fixture-tenant and fixture-user, with deadline 60. Step 1: send event fixture-approved with status Approved and policy true. Expect status approved, deadline 60, permission_granted true, grant_count 1, live_permission_changed false. Step 2: replay fixture-approved. Expect the identical object. The duplicate is a no-op. Step 3: send a new event ID, for example fixture-correction, with status Declined. Expect status declined, deadline 60, permission_granted false, grant_count 1, live_permission_changed false. The tested expired output is a different path: a session that never received an approval. It has status expired, permission_granted false, grant_count 0, next review_or_authorized_provider_refresh and provider_polled false. Do not use it as evidence of revocation. New correction, duplicate, or stale pending event Three inputs can look alike and must stay distinct. A new correction carries an unseen event ID and status Declined against an approved session. It revokes the permission. A duplicate reuses a processed event ID. It returns stored state, even if its status field now differs. A stale pending event, such as In Progress or In Review arriving after Approved, must not downgrade or re-grant anything. The fixture returns current state and does not record it. Two more cases follow the same rule. A late Approved after a Declined correction is also ignored, so permission does not silently reopen. A second Declined after declined changes nothing. Test each case with distinct event IDs and assert both permission_granted and grant_count. Proposed design: a caller-owned revocation receipt The following is a proposed design, not fixture behavior. The fixture flips one flag; real revocation touches listings, payouts or sessions in systems you own. A caller-owned revocation receipt could record: the session the correcting event ID the previous and new status the grant count at revocation a timestamp which downstream actions were requested and confirmed Write the receipt in the same transaction that clears the permission. Make downstream undo steps idempotent against that receipt. Before trusting a correction, re-fetch the authoritative decision through an authorized provider route. A synthetic Declined is not evidence of a real decline, and synthetic fixture permission is not live business permission. Failure handling Several failures need defined behavior. If a correction fails the binding check, the fixture raises BINDING_MISMATCH. Treat this as an alert, not as a revocation. Non-synthetic sources raise PRODUCTION_SIGNATURE_VERIFIER_NOT_IMPLEMENTED. Event IDs without the fixture- prefix raise SYNTHETIC_EVENT_REQUIRED. Sending an event for an unknown session raises BINDING_MISMATCH; reading an unknown session with read raises SESSION_NOT_FOUND. The recover method only expires pending, review or unknown sessions locally. It never polls a provider and never reverses an approval. Do not rely on it to catch a missed correction. If your downstream revocation partially fails, keep the permission cleared and mark the receipt incomplete for review. Do not restore access. Acceptance checklist Approved with policy true yields permission_granted true and grant_count 1. A replayed approval event ID leaves both fields unchanged. A new Declined event yields status declined, permission_granted false and grant_count 1. Stale In Progress or In Review after Approved changes nothing. A late Approved after the correction does not restore permission. A correction with the wrong tenant or subject is rejected. live_permission_changed stays false throughout. Your own receipt and downstream undo steps are tested separately. Your correction semantics are confirmed against the real provider contract before any live use. This local example makes no network calls. title: Should an unknown phone result reject a signup?
author: murray wang
summary: A signup form calls a phone check and gets back something that is neither valid nor invalid. Either the result is unknown or the provider call failed. The tempting shortcut is to reject anything other than a clean pass. This article argues against that shortcut and walks through the four-branch synthetic example to show how to route each outcome. The core distinction is simple. An unknown result is missing evidence, not negative evidence. If you reject on missing evidence, every provider outage becomes a user lockout. The problem and the decision you own The decision in front of you is not whether a number is good. It is what your signup flow should do when the check cannot answer. Three outcomes look alike in code but mean different things. A confirmed invalid number is evidence. An unknown result means the check returned no usable signal. A provider failure means the check never completed. Only the first justifies blocking on format grounds. The other two need an explicit path: bounded recovery, manual review, or a possession step through an OTP provider you already run. Keep in mind what no phone check establishes. Validity and line type are different from possession and identity. The current free production route does not request line type, ownership, reachability or OTP delivery. Its approved controlled pilot covers basic number format and validity only. What the downloadable example implements The downloadable example runs offline in Python 3.10 or later. It needs no credentials and makes no network calls. It has four branches: normal, unknown, provider_failure and otp. Every output includes the fields mode, branch, state, valid, line_type, next, otp_sent and live_line_type_available. Two values never change across branches. The mode field is always synthetic_fixture. The otp_sent field is always false, so the example never sends a code. The live_line_type_available field is always false, which reflects that the free route does not return line type. The mobile line type you will see in the normal branch is fixture data, not something a live check would return. Any branch name outside the four raises UNSUPPORTED_FIXTURE. This example is not the same as the anonymous HTTP trial, which covers three scenarios. Do not treat results from one as results from the other. Worked hypothetical: four signups, four routes Imagine a hypothetical marketplace that receives four signups in one hour. The fixture's expected outputs map onto them as follows. The first signup takes the normal branch. The output is state simulated, valid true, line_type mobile and next continue_customer_policy. Your own rules decide what happens next. The check alone does not admit the user. The second signup takes the unknown branch. The output is state unknown, valid null, line_type null and next review_or_existing_otp. The account is held for review or sent to your existing OTP step. It is not rejected. The third signup takes the provider_failure branch. The output is also state unknown with valid null and line_type null, but next is bounded_retry_then_review. You retry a limited number of times and then hand the case to review. The fourth signup takes the otp branch, which models a request to prove possession. The output is state unsupported, valid null, line_type null and next customer_otp_provider. GridZen sends nothing here. That step belongs to your OTP provider. All four outputs carry otp_sent false. Proposed application design for failure handling The following is design guidance for your application, not behavior the fixture implements. Bound retries with a fixed attempt count and a deadline, so a provider failure cannot loop forever or block the form indefinitely. Store unknown and failed outcomes as their own state, kept separate from invalid. That way, reviewers and analytics do not mistake an outage for fraud. When review is the route, decide what the user may do while pending. You might let them browse but block payouts or listings until the case is resolved. If you route to OTP, call your existing provider and record its result separately from the phone check result. Do not let a null valid value coerce to false anywhere in your code. Limits you should state plainly The fixture produces synthetic outputs only. It proves branch handling in your code, not production success. Its tests cover simulated transitions, bindings, duplicate callbacks, restart and timeouts. They do not demonstrate live accuracy, external adoption or agent superiority. An OTP recommendation does not send a code and does not establish possession. Live route availability requires separate confirmation. Production phone checks are limited to the controlled pilot, and self-service live verification is disabled. Acceptance checklist Before you ship, confirm each of the following. Running all four branches reproduces exactly the next values listed above. Your code treats a null valid value as unknown, never as invalid. The unknown branch never auto-rejects a signup. The provider_failure branch retries a bounded number of times, then moves to review. The otp branch calls only your own OTP provider and records otp_sent as false on the GridZen side. No logic reads line_type from a live result. Your code handles UNSUPPORTED_FIXTURE. The unit tests pass. Documentation does not claim ownership, reachability or identity from a phone check. Run the checked synthetic example Download and extract https://gridzen.ai/downloads/verification-delivery.zip , enter verification_delivery, then run with Python 3.10+. This local example makes no network calls. title: File Handling in Python
author: Lameck Odhiambo
summary: File handling in Python is important as it allows you to create, read, update, and delete files directly from your code. Python manages these operations using a built-in open() function, which creates a file object to interact with the file system. with Statement This is best practice and recommended method for opening files in Python is using the with keyword. It automatically closes the file once the block of code finishes, even if errors occur. This prevents memory leaks and file corruption. # The file closes automatically outside this block with open ( " example.txt " , " r " ) as file : content = file . read () print ( content ) File Open Modes The second argument of open() specifies the "mode" (how you want to interact with the file) • "r" ( Read ): Default mode. Opens a file for reading. Throws a FileNotFoundError if the file doesn't exist. • "w" ( Write ): Opens a file for writing. Overwrites existing content. Creates a new file if it doesn't exist. • "a" ( Append ): Opens a file to add data to the end. It does not erase existing content. Creates a new file if it doesn't exist. • "x" ( Create ): Creates a specific file. Returns an error if the file already exists. Reading Files .txt Python provides several methods to extract text from an open file: • read(size) : Reads the entire file as a single string. You can pass an optional integer size to read only a specific number of characters. • readline() : Reads just one line at a time. Helpful for reading large files line by line. • readlines() : Reads all lines at once and returns them as a list of strings. • Line Loop (Efficient) : You can iterate directly over the file object using a loop, which is memory-efficient for large files. # Reading line-by-line efficiently with open ( " large_file.txt " , " r " ) as file : for line in file : print ( line . strip ()) # strip() removes extra newlines # Reading entire content at once with open ( " example.txt " , " r " , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as file : content = file . read () print ( content ) .json Python converts JSON data directly into dictionaries and lists import json with open ( ' data.json ' , ' r ' ) as file : data = json . load ( file ) print ( data ) .csv import csv with open ( ' data.csv ' , mode = ' r ' , encoding = ' utf-8 ' ) as file : # Create the reader object reader = csv . reader ( file ) # Optional: Skip the header row if your file has one header = next ( reader ) for row in reader : # Each row is a list. Access columns by index (e.g., row[0]) print ( row ) Writing Files .txt To add content, open the file in write ("w") or append ("a") mode: • write(string) : Inserts a string into the file. • writelines(list) : Inserts a list of strings into the file all at once lines_to_write = [ " First line \n " , " Second line \n " ] with open ( " output.txt " , " w " ) as file : file . writelines ( lines_to_write ) .json import json # Your data structure (Python dictionary) user_data = { " name " : " Alice Smith " , " age " : 30 , " active " : True , " roles " : [ " admin " , " user " ] } # Writing to a file with open ( " user.json " , " w " ) as file : json . dump ( user_data , file ) .csv import csv # Data structured as a list of lists (rows) data = [ [ " Name " , " Age " , " City " ], [ " Alice " , 30 , " New York " ], [ " Bob " , 25 , " Los Angeles " ], [ " Charlie " , 35 , " Chicago " ] ] # Open the file in write mode ('w') with open ( ' output.csv ' , mode = ' w ' , newline = '' , encoding = ' utf-8 ' ) as file : writer = csv . writer ( file ) # Write all rows at once writer . writerows ( data ) Deleting and Deleting Files For file system operations like deleting or renaming, you need to import Python's built-in os module import os # Delete a file safely if os . path . exists ( " old_file.txt " ): os . remove ( " old_file.txt " ) Conclusion File handling is critical because it enables data persistence, allowing programs to save information permanently to a storage disk so it isn't lost when the application closes or the system powers down. It serves as a universal bridge for software interoperability, letting different systems exchange data using standardized formats like CSV or JSON, and allows programs to efficiently stream massive datasets that are too large to fit into a computer's temporary memory (RAM). Additionally, it is essential for maintaining application configuration settings and generating long-term audit logs, making it a foundational tool for building functional, scalable, and secure software.

title: Your retry logic has never seen a real 429. Here is how to test it with a local fault-injecting mock
author: rene
summary: Most LLM client code has a retry branch that has never actually run. The provider returns 200 in every test, so the 429 , 500 and timeout paths sit untested until production hits them at 3am. The fix is cheap: point your client at a local server that fails on a schedule you control. The idea Run a tiny HTTP server on localhost that mimics a chat-completions endpoint. Give it a failure schedule, for example: [ { "status" : 429 , "retry_after" : 2 }, { "status" : 500 }, { "status" : "timeout" }, { "status" : 200 } ] Each incoming request consumes the next step. Your client sees a 429 with a Retry-After header, then a 500, then a hang, then a good response. What to assert Retry-After is honored. The second attempt should not fire before the header says it can. There is a time budget. The loop gives up after N seconds, not after infinity. Timeouts are set. A hung request raises instead of blocking forever. Non-retryable errors fail fast. A 400 should not be retried. Backoff has jitter. Two clients should not retry in lockstep. A minimal version import json , sys , time from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler , HTTPServer SCHEDULE = json . load ( open ( sys . argv [ 1 ])) step = { " i " : 0 } class H ( BaseHTTPRequestHandler ): def do_POST ( self ): s = SCHEDULE [ min ( step [ " i " ], len ( SCHEDULE ) - 1 )] step [ " i " ] += 1 if s [ " status " ] == " timeout " : time . sleep ( 60 ) return self . send_response ( s [ " status " ]) if " retry_after " in s : self . send_header ( " Retry-After " , str ( s [ " retry_after " ])) self . end_headers () self . wfile . write ( b ' { " choices " :[{ " message " :{ " content " : " ok " }}]} ' ) HTTPServer (( " 127.0.0.1 " , 9797 ), H ). serve_forever () Point your client's base URL at http://127.0.0.1:9797 and run your normal code path. If you want it packaged I bundled a slightly more complete version (schedule file, README, examples) as a pay-what-you-want download, minimum $1: https://renevibe76.gumroad.com/l/sargxm The snippet above is enough to get started on your own, though. The point is to see your retry code run at least once before production does it for you.

title: Why Is My Base44 App Not Working? What 192 Real Reports Say
author: Tushar Bhendarkar
summary: More than one in five people who said their Base44 app had stopped working had done nothing wrong. I went through 192 public reports of broken Base44 apps, from Reddit, Base44's own feedback board, Trustpilot and YouTube, and sorted each one by what actually caused it. The biggest group, 42 reports, was Base44 itself having an outage. I did this because Base44 keeps coming up in the freelance work I look at: founders who built something real with it, then got stuck. Before telling anyone how to fix their app, I wanted to know what actually breaks. The outage number matters because the usual reaction is to ask Base44's AI to fix the app. During an outage that can't work. It costs credits, and it can break code that was fine. Base44's own docs say credits aren't refunded when the AI gets something wrong. So below are the causes in the order I'd check them, with the fix for each from Base44's documentation. If your app works but isn't showing up in Google, skip to the last section: I ran 45 live Base44 apps through my free checkers, and 8 of them were telling Google not to index them. What 192 broken Base44 apps had in common The reports run from August 2025 to October 2026: 88 Reddit threads, 73 posts on Base44's public feedback board, 16 Trustpilot reviews, and a handful from X, YouTube, GitHub, Hacker News and elsewhere. I put each one in a group based on the cause the thread confirmed, or the fix that worked. The single biggest cause was Base44 itself being down. Login problems and preview-only issues come next. What surprised me is how little of this is code. Three groups make up almost half of the list: Base44 outages, login and sign-up problems, and issues that only exist in the editor preview or your browser's cache. You don't fix any of those by rewriting your app. The rest are real problems in an app's settings or code, and many of them come down to a setting you can check in a few minutes. In 22 reports the cause was never found, or didn't fit any group. Step 1: make sure it is not Base44, or your network This is the step people skip. Before you touch the app, open status.base44.com and the r/Base44 subreddit. Base44's status feed lists 26 incidents between December 2025 and September 2026, five of them affecting previews or published apps. In the reports, people sometimes posted about an outage on Reddit before the status page showed anything. If your app and other people's apps broke at the same time, wait before you change anything. When an outage ends, your browser can keep showing the old loading screen. After its September 9, 2026 incident, Base44 told users: "If you still see Loading your app, refresh the page or clear your browser cache." A hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R, or Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac) or a private window is the quickest test. Then I'd open the app on a phone using mobile data, not Wi-Fi. Four of the reports turned out to be the visitor's internet provider blocking base44.app addresses: Comcast Xfinity's Advanced Security feature in the US, and an internet provider in the Philippines. The app was fine. Those visitors just couldn't reach it until they switched network or used a VPN. Step 2: work out which kind of "not working" you have "Not working" covers very different problems, and the fix depends on which one you have. Find the line that matches what you see, then jump to its section below. What you see Most likely causes Check first Nothing loads, for anyone, you included Base44 outage, or a stale cache after one Status page, hard refresh, another network It loads for you but not for others Not published, set to Private, a custom domain, or the visitor's network App Visibility and the Publish button It works in the preview, not in the live app Not republished, test data, a backend function not redeployed Publish panel, test data switch Login, sign-up or Google sign-in fails Login settings, emails in spam, Google OAuth setup Login settings, spam folder Data is missing or will not save Data permissions, or a field that does not match its table "Act as a user", App Logs It worked yesterday, broke after an AI change The AI edit itself The Revert button, Version History Emails, AI features or payments stopped Credits ran out, plan limits, API keys Credits page, plan, Secrets Base44 also has a built-in check: type "Something is wrong" in the AI chat and it runs a diagnosis. Read what it says, but don't let it make several rounds of changes before you know the cause. It works in the preview but not when published The editor preview and the live app are two different things. According to Base44's editor docs , the live app only changes when you click Publish, and the preview is visible only to you and your collaborators. So my first question is always the boring one: did you click Publish after the change, and did you see the success message? Test data is not real data On the Builder plan and up, the preview can use a separate test database. The published app always uses real (production) data, and the two are completely separate, so records you created while testing will never appear in the live app. Base44 explains this on its test data page . Backend functions and the browser cache Base44's troubleshooting guide has an official checklist for when published changes don't appear: clear the browser cache, try another browser or device, confirm you clicked Publish, redeploy any backend function you changed, and check the error logs. A backend function you edited keeps running its old version until it's redeployed. Sixteen reports were problems that existed only in the editor preview or the browser cache, such as a preview that kept going white after every AI change while the live app worked. Revert the last change first. If both the preview and the live app fail with a 500 error, Base44's guide calls that a server-side problem the builder usually can't fix, and that one is for support. It loads for you but not for your users This is the most confusing one, because everything looks fine when you test it. As the owner, you can see things your users can't. Check App Visibility Every app has a visibility setting in Dashboard, then Overview, then App Visibility: Public (anyone, no sign-in), Private (only people you invited) or Workspace (only your Base44 workspace). People who weren't invited to a Private app see an error or a request-access pop-up. Private applies to every page, including a landing page, and since February 6, 2026 new Private apps need the Starter plan or higher. The details are on Base44's access page . Invites also do nothing until the app is published, so an invited person can still be locked out of an unpublished app. Data that only you can see On any app with user accounts, this is the one I'd check first. Base44 protects each table with data permissions, and a blocked read doesn't show an error. Its security docs say a denied read behaves as if the data doesn't exist: the list just comes back empty. So a page can be full for you and empty for a normal user, with nothing in the console. The built-in Users table is a common trap: only the owner and collaborators can read it, so member profiles and leaderboards work for you and break for everyone else. To see what a normal user sees, use "Act as a user" or "Test Permissions in preview", and run the Security scan, which flags missing or wrong rules. If saving fails with a 403 error, the user doesn't have permission to write to that table. Custom domains Ten reports were custom domain problems: stuck on "Pending verification", or a Bad Gateway error on the domain while the base44.app address worked. Base44's domain guide says to remove any AAAA (IPv6) records, allow up to 48 hours, and, if your DNS is on Cloudflare, set Base44's records to "DNS only" (grey cloud). Proxying them through Cloudflare can cause SSL errors and pages that load on base44.app but not on your domain. I always test the base44.app address first: if that works, the problem is the domain, not the app. Login and sign-up problems Login failures were the second biggest group, with 27 reports: verification codes that never arrived, invites that skipped the set-password step, Google sign-in errors and redirect loops. Base44's login docs cover the common causes: Emails in spam. Verification and reset emails come from no-reply@base44-apps.com unless you set up your own sending domain. Ask users to check spam and allowlist that address. A renamed reset page. Apps built since June 2026 have their own login pages, and the reset link always points to /reset-password. If the forgot-password or reset-password page is renamed or deleted, password resets break. Google sign-in. By default the Google window says base44.com. Showing your own domain needs the Builder plan, a connected custom domain, the right redirect address and Google's approval, which can take up to five days. Self sign-up on a Private app. If people can register but then see access denied, the app is probably Private. Make it Public and protect the pages that need a login. It worked yesterday, and an AI edit broke it Fifteen reports describe the same loop: the app worked, someone asked the AI for a change or a fix, and something else broke. Each new fix broke something new and spent more credits. The most important rule comes from Base44's own troubleshooting guide: asking the AI chat to revert never undoes anything. Only the Revert button on a message, or Version History, rolls the app back. Base44 also advises trying the automatic fix once or twice, then switching to Discuss mode (about 0.3 credits a message) to describe the problem instead of letting the AI keep editing. One warning if you use GitHub sync: after you connect it, Version History can't restore versions from before the connection. This is the group that worries me most, because the worst report in it wasn't a crash. In a client portal built on Base44, the AI "fixed" a display bug by changing how files were looked up, and two weeks after launch one company could see another company's files. Nothing looked broken, which is why nobody noticed. When I built Client Approvals , I wrote a test that checks one workspace can never see another workspace's requests. After any AI change that touches data, that's the check I'd run by hand: sign in as a normal user and look at what they can see. Features that quietly stop: credits, plans and keys Some failures look like bugs but are really limits. Base44 has two kinds of credits, explained on its credits page : message credits, spent when the AI builds or edits your app, and integration credits, spent when the live app uses Base44's built-in services such as email, AI calls and file uploads. Running out doesn't take the app down. Actions that use credits pause until your next reset. Since August 27, 2026 every email the app sends uses integration credits, so at the limit, workflow emails fail. Reading and writing your own data never uses credits. Credits are shared. They come from one pool for the whole workspace, so one busy app can use them up for all your apps. The Free plan is capped at 5 credits a day. Some features need a plan. Backend functions need the Builder plan or higher. Downgrading, or a disputed card payment that moves the workspace to Free, stops them, along with every integration that depends on them. Keys and webhooks. API keys for other services go in Secrets. In one report, a function kept using an old key after it was changed, until the app was republished. Webhooks from services that can't sign in, such as Telegram or WhatsApp, return 403 unless the function is public. Not showing up on Google? What I found on 45 live Base44 apps Sometimes "not showing" means the app works fine but can't be found or shared. I build free website checkers, so I wanted to see how live Base44 apps look from the outside. I took 45 of them from Base44's own showcase, its templates and Hacker News posts, ran each one through my sitemap checker , Open Graph checker and security headers checker , and fetched each home page the way Googlebot does. Eight apps their makers had shared publicly were telling Google not to index them. Eight of the 45 apps sent Google a noindex instruction on their home page, which tells search engines to leave the page out of their results. These were apps their makers had shared publicly. Base44's SEO docs describe the usual source: switching off the main SEO setting adds noindex and stops Base44 from writing your page content into the version crawlers read. Three more apps showed Google a page with no text on it at all. If your app isn't showing up in Google, check that setting first. The same docs say Base44's search features (sitemap, robots.txt and social previews) are built for apps on a custom domain. The free base44.app address can be crawled, but it isn't meant for search traffic, so if Google matters to you, connect your own domain. Share previews were mostly there but often weak. Base44 builds them from the title, description and logo in your app settings, which is why many apps share a square logo, and many apps show a square image as a small thumbnail instead of a large card. Nineteen of the 40 share images were over 300 KB, and WhatsApp often skips images that big. My Open Graph checker shows exactly what your link looks like before you post it. On security, Base44 sets HTTPS correctly for every app, but 44 of 45 sent no Content-Security-Policy, the header that limits which scripts a page may run. When to stop prompting and get help Work through the causes in order: Base44 and your network first, then who can see the app, then its data and logins, and only then the code. It's the same rule I use for chatbots that give wrong answers : find the stage that breaks, and fix only that. If you need Base44 support, send them the app link, the time it happened, the errors from your browser console and what App Logs shows (Dashboard, then Logs, with the Errors only filter). Their guide asks for exactly that. If you're thinking of leaving Base44, know what export gives you. Downloading the code or syncing it to GitHub needs the Builder plan, and you get a standard React and Vite project. But that code still talks to Base44 for your data, logins and backend functions, so moving off Base44 means rebuilding the backend, not just downloading files. More guides like this one are in Fix an AI-built app . And if you'd rather hand it over, I take these on as client projects: send me the app link and what's broken. Common questions Why is my Base44 app stuck on "Loading your app"? Most often because Base44 itself is having trouble: check status.base44.com and the r/Base44 subreddit. If the outage is over and you still see the loading screen, do a hard refresh or clear your browser cache, which is what Base44 told users after its September 2026 incident. If it only fails on one network, try mobile data, because some internet providers have blocked base44.app addresses. Why does my Base44 app work in the preview but not when published? The live app only changes when you click Publish, so the usual cause is an edit that was never published. If you use test data, the preview reads a separate test database while the live app always uses real data. Backend functions also need to be redeployed after changes, and a stale browser cache can show an old version. Why can other people not open my Base44 app? Check that the app is published and that App Visibility (Dashboard, Overview) is set to Public. A Private app only lets in people you invited, and invites do nothing until the app is published. If you use a custom domain, test the free base44.app address too, and ask the person to try another network. Why is data missing for some users of my Base44 app? Usually data permissions. When a permission rule blocks someone from reading a table, Base44 returns an empty list with no error, so the page looks empty to them while it looks fine to you as the owner. The built-in Users table can only be read by the owner and collaborators, which breaks member profiles and leaderboards for regular users. Does a Base44 app stop working when credits run out? The app stays live, but features that use credits pause until your credits reset: built-in email, AI calls, file uploads and similar. Reading and writing your app's own data does not use credits. Credits are shared across every app in the workspace, so one busy app can use them up for all of them. Why is my Base44 app not showing up on Google? Check that the app is not telling Google to stay away: Base44 adds a noindex tag when its main SEO setting is switched off, and 8 of 45 live apps I checked had one. Base44's search features are also built for apps on a custom domain rather than the free base44.app address. Can I export my Base44 app and host it myself? You can download the code or sync it to GitHub on the Builder plan or higher, and you get a standard React and Vite project. But it still talks to Base44 for data, logins and backend functions, so moving fully off Base44 means rebuilding that backend, not just downloading the code. This post first appeared on tusharbhendarkar.com . I fix apps built with Lovable, Replit, Bolt and Base44, and I build free checkers for live apps. If something here is broken for you, email me at tusharbhendarkar44@gmail.com .

title: Best email subject lines for online course launch
author: BAW BAN
summary: Best Email Subject Lines for Online Course Launch: 12 Proven Formulas (With Examples) You've built the course. You've recorded the modules. The sales page is live. And now you're staring at a blank subject line field, wondering why the hardest part of launching feels like writing twelve words. Subject lines decide whether your launch emails get opened—and if they don't get opened, nothing else in your funnel matters. According to widely cited email marketing benchmarks, subject lines are one of the single biggest factors in open rates, and open rates directly cap your click-throughs, conversions, and revenue. This guide breaks down the best email subject lines for an online course launch by category, with real examples you can adapt, plus a quick testing framework so you're not guessing. Why Subject Lines Matter More During a Course Launch A course launch isn't a single email—it's a sequence. Typically you're sending: A "doors are open" announcement 2–4 value/objection-handling emails A cart-close reminder (often 2–3 of them) If your open rate drops from 40% to 25% across that sequence, you don't lose 15% of your sales—you lose it at every single touchpoint. That compounds fast. The good news: launch emails have a built-in advantage. Your list opted in for this topic, and there's a real deadline. Subject lines that lean into curiosity, specificity, and urgency consistently outperform generic ones. The 12 Best Email Subject Lines for an Online Course Launch (By Category) 1. Curiosity-Driven Subject Lines These work early in the launch, when you want clicks from people who aren't yet sold. "The mistake I made before my first launch" "Why most [topic] courses fail (it's not the content)" "I almost didn't publish this" "What changed after I stopped doing [common tactic]" Why they work: They open a loop the reader wants closed. Avoid clickbait that the email body doesn't pay off—that trains your list to ignore you. 2. Benefit & Outcome Subject Lines Best for the value emails mid-launch. "From [painful before state] to [desired after state] in 30 days" "How to [specific outcome] without [common obstacle]" "The 3-step system for [result]" Example: "How to fill your first cohort without a huge audience" Specificity beats hype. "Change your life" gets ignored; "fill your first cohort" gets clicked. 3. Urgency & Deadline Subject Lines Reserve these for the final 24–48 hours. "Doors close tonight at midnight" "Last call: [Course name] enrollment ends in 6 hours" "Quick reminder before we close" Important: Only use real deadlines. Fake scarcity erodes trust faster than it generates sales. 4. Social Proof & Story Subject Lines "[Student name] went from [before] to [after]" "How [Name] landed [result] in [timeframe]" "The email that made me finally buy [type of product]" Testimonials in subject lines work especially well for warm audiences who've seen your earlier emails. 5. Objection-Handling Subject Lines "Is [course] right for you? Here's the honest answer" "'I don't have time' — let's talk about that" "What if it doesn't work for your situation?" These often get lower open rates but higher conversion rates, because they attract people with real buying intent. 6 Quick Formulas You Can Reuse Formula Template Example The Mistake "The [mistake] that [negative outcome]" "The pricing mistake that killed my first launch" The Shortcut "[Outcome] without [pain]" "Launch emails without writing from scratch" The Deadline "[Action] closes [time]" "Enrollment closes Friday" The Question "Are you making this [topic] mistake?" "Are you making this launch email mistake?" The Number "[N] ways to [outcome]" "5 subject lines that doubled my opens" The Story "How [person] got [result]" "How Dana sold 40 seats in 4 days" A 5-Step Checklist Before You Hit Send Is it under ~50 characters? Mobile clients truncate around there. Does it avoid spam triggers? (ALL CAPS, "FREE!!!", excessive emoji) Does the email body deliver on the promise? Mismatch = unsubscribes. Is it distinct from your last 3 subject lines? Repeating patterns = fatigue. Does it match the launch stage? Curiosity early, urgency late. The Real Problem: Writing 12+ Subject Lines Per Launch Here's the part most course creators underestimate. A launch isn't one subject line—it's a full sequence. You need: 5–7 launch emails 2–3 subject line variations each (for A/B testing) Consistent messaging that ties into your sales page That's 15–20 subject lines, plus the emails themselves, plus the sales page, plus social posts. And all of it has to sound like you , not a template. If that's the bottleneck, the «Course Launch Copy Kit» was built for exactly this stage—when the course is done but the copy isn't. It's a $49 template pack with proven frameworks, swipe files, and step-by-step prompts for your sales page, launch emails, and social posts. Instead of staring at a blank doc, you fill in the blanks. How to A/B Test Subject Lines (Without Overthinking It) You don't need enterprise software. Here's a simple approach: Split your list into two segments (most email tools do this natively). Send two subject lines to each half at the same time. Wait 4–6 hours , then check open rates. Send the winning version to non-openers with a "did you see this?" angle. Test one variable at a time : length, emoji vs. no emoji, question vs. statement. If you change three things at once, you learn nothing. Common Subject Line Mistakes That Kill Launch Emails Being too clever. If the reader has to decode it, they'll skip it. Vague urgency. "Don't miss out!" means nothing. "Closes tonight" means something. Ignoring mobile. Preview text matters as much as the subject line—write both. No personalization at all. Even just a first name can lift opens. Overusing emojis. One is fine. Five looks like spam. Same tone across the whole sequence. Vary it: curiosity → value → proof → urgency. Putting It Together: A Sample Launch Sequence Here's how the categories map to a 7-email launch: Day 1 – Announcement: "Doors are open: [Course name]" Day 2 – Value: "How to [outcome] without [obstacle]" Day 3 – Story: "[Student] got [result] in [time]" Day 4 – Objection: "Is this right for you? Honest answer inside" Day 5 – Proof: "3 people, 3 different results" Day 6 – Urgency: "Closes tomorrow at midnight" Day 7 – Final call: "Last chance — closing in 6 hours" Each of these can be A/B tested with a second version. That's 14 subject lines for one launch—and a much higher chance of hitting the ones your audience actually opens. Final Take The best email subject lines for an online course launch aren't the cleverest ones—they're the ones that match your reader's stage, promise something specific, and get delivered on inside the email. title: A reproducible acceptance checklist for a browser photo editor
author: NiceDayUp
summary: When somebody recommends a browser editing tool, it is easy to ask the wrong question first: does it look like the desktop application you already know? A more useful question is whether you can reproduce one complete task, including getting a usable file back out. Craft Apps provides a concrete example for designing that check. Its collection includes PhotoCraft for image work, and the PhotoCraft page publishes limits that should shape an evaluation. I inspected the live pages, waited for the editor to load and opened its new-document dialog. I did not complete an import, edit or export test. The procedure below is an acceptance plan that you can run with your own material. Make the test case smaller than the real job Choose a source image that you are allowed to edit and keep it unchanged. Create a separate copy for the trial. Write down the intended output dimensions, where the image will be displayed and the one property you plan to change. For example, an announcement image with a short title gives you a simple visual requirement: the title should remain readable at the final display size. This is a proposed test case, not an image created during this inspection. Avoid adding unrelated tasks to it. If the first question is typography, a complex layered import will introduce extra variables before you have an answer. The photocraft page describes a layered workspace and PSD-oriented work, but it explicitly warns that some PSD features may not translate perfectly. Use a separate compatibility case when a particular layer structure or effect is essential. Record the current preflight controls Let the editor finish its initial download. In this inspection, the loaded start screen offered New document and Open. Opening New document exposed width, height, resolution, color mode, bit depth and background choices. These are observed interface controls; they are not evidence that a document has been created successfully. Record the controls relevant to your case before continuing. If the available options do not support your intended task, stop the trial and write down the mismatch. That is already a useful finding. You do not need to force a different workflow just to produce a positive result. Keep the product-page demonstrations separate from these observations. The site labels its screenshots as upstream examples and says the web build may differ. A screenshot can explain what a feature is for without establishing its behavior in the version you opened. Test the file boundary explicitly The product page says the browser build opens files through the file picker and saves by download. It also says that web autosave and crash recovery are unavailable. Those statements make a short trial and a deliberate save step especially useful. After making the intended change, use a save or export option that the current build offers. Locate the download, record its format and reopen it. Check the dimensions and the visual property in the brief. If continued editing is required, also check whether the reopened version preserves the structure you need. A preview, a completed download and a reusable working file are separate observations. Do not combine them into a single “works” checkbox. If the downloaded result looks correct but cannot support later editing, that may be acceptable for one job and unsuitable for another. Keep a result that another person could inspect A short evaluation note can contain the source filename, the intended change, the controls used, the save option and the reopened result. Attach a small screenshot when it explains a discrepancy. Record what remains untested instead of inferring broader compatibility from a narrow pass. For this preflight, the editor and new-document dialog loaded. Import fidelity, editing behavior, file output and recovery were not independently verified. That is the boundary of the available evidence. Use the checklist to decide whether the current browser build supports your actual task. One reproducible file workflow is a stronger basis for that decision than a long list of familiar-looking tools.

title: What to include in a course sales page to increase conversions
author: BAW BAN
summary: What to Include in a Course Sales Page to Increase Conversions You've built the course. You've recorded the lessons, uploaded the modules, and set up the checkout. Now you're staring at a blank sales page wondering why the words won't come—and why, when they do, visitors still aren't buying. The gap between "good course" and "course that sells" is almost always the sales page. And the good news is that a high-converting sales page isn't about clever writing. It's about structure. When you know what to include in a course sales page to increase conversions, you stop guessing and start building a page that does the selling for you. Here's a practical, section-by-section breakdown you can apply today. 1. A Headline That Names the Transformation Your headline has one job: make the right person feel seen in under five seconds. Weak headlines describe the course ("An 8-Week Course on Freelance Writing"). Strong headlines describe the outcome ("Go From Zero Clients to a Waitlist in 8 Weeks—Without Cold Pitching"). A simple formula that works: [End result] + [timeframe or method] + [for whom] Test it against this question: Would my ideal student read this and think "that's me"? If not, rewrite it. Avoid vague words like "mastery," "journey," and "unlock your potential"—they say nothing specific. 2. A Subheadline That Kills the Main Objection The subheadline is where you address the biggest reason people hesitate. Common objections: "I don't have time." "I've tried courses before and never finished." "I'm not technical enough." Example subheadline: "Built for busy parents—short lessons, lifetime access, and a template for every step." 3. The "Who This Is For" Block Conversions rise when people can quickly self-identify. Write two short lists: This is for you if… (3–5 bullets describing your ideal student's situation) This is NOT for you if… (2–3 bullets that filter out mismatches) The second list builds trust. It signals you're not trying to sell to everyone—which makes the right buyer more confident. 4. The Problem → Agitation → Solution Sequence Before you present the course, walk the reader through their current pain. Use concrete language: Problem: "You've got a finished course but no idea how to write the sales page." Agitation: "Every day it sits unpublished is a day you're not getting paid—and the longer you wait, the harder it feels to start." Solution: "Here's a proven structure you can fill in, section by section." This is the emotional core of the page. Skip it and your course feels like a feature list instead of a fix. 5. A Clear Course Overview (What's Inside) Buyers want to know exactly what they're getting. Break it down: Module-by-module list with a one-line benefit for each Total length and format (video, audio, PDF, live calls) Bonuses and their standalone value Access details (lifetime? drip? community?) Keep each module description focused on the result , not the topic . "Module 3: Write Emails That Get Clicks" beats "Module 3: Email Marketing." 6. Instructor Credibility You don't need to be famous. You need to be relevant . Include: A short bio focused on why you're qualified to teach this specific topic 1–2 concrete results or case studies A photo (real faces convert better than logos) If you have testimonials from beta students, put them here. 7. Social Proof: Testimonials and Results Place testimonials near the claims they support , not just in one lump at the bottom. If you claim "you'll finish in 4 weeks," put a student quote about finishing right next to it. Best testimonial format: Result + specific detail + name/photo Example: "I wrote my entire sales page in one afternoon using the module 2 framework. Launched to $2,400 in the first week." — Sarah M. No testimonials yet? Use beta feedback, screenshots of student messages, or your own before/after story. 8. Pricing That Justifies Itself Don't just drop a number. Frame it: Anchor the value: What would it cost to hire someone to do this? What's the cost of staying stuck? Show the price clearly with what's included Offer a payment plan if the price is over $100 State your guarantee (refund window, conditions) A simple line like "30-day money-back guarantee—if you do the work and don't get results, email us for a full refund" removes enormous friction. 9. A Strong, Repeated CTA Your call-to-action should appear at least 3 times on the page: After the headline/hero section After the "what's inside" section After the guarantee/FAQ Use action-based button text: "Enroll Now," "Get Instant Access," "Start Today." Avoid "Learn More" or "Submit." And make sure the button stands out visually. 10. An FAQ That Handles Last-Minute Doubts The FAQ is where you close the sale for fence-sitters. Answer the real questions: How long do I have access? What if I'm a beginner? Is there a refund policy? How much time do I need per week? Do I get support? Write the answers as if you're talking to a friend—direct, honest, no fluff. 11. A Final "Two Futures" Close End the page with a short paragraph contrasting two outcomes: Future A: Nothing changes. The course stays unfinished, the sales page stays unwritten. Future B: You follow the structure, publish the page, and start enrolling students. Then place your final CTA button. This is the last emotional push—keep it warm, not pushy. A Quick Pre-Launch Checklist Before you publish, run through this: [ ] Headline names a specific outcome [ ] Subheadline addresses the top objection [ ] "Who it's for / not for" lists are clear [ ] Problem → Agitation → Solution is present [ ] Every module has a benefit, not just a topic [ ] At least 3 testimonials or proof points [ ] Pricing is framed with value and a guarantee [ ] CTA appears 3+ times with action verbs [ ] FAQ answers the 5 most common objections [ ] Page ends with a "two futures" close When the Writing Itself Is the Bottleneck Knowing what to include in a course sales page to increase conversions is one thing. Actually writing each section—headline, emails, social posts, FAQ—is where most course creators stall out for weeks. That's exactly the problem «Course Launch Copy Kit» was built to solve.
